upright: You are standing at the base of a problem you have never touched. You do not have the beta. You do not know where the feet go. The Fool steps off the cliff not from carelessness but from willingness — the white rose is your beginner's mind, the knapsack holds only what you actually need. Pull on. See where the rock takes you before you ask anyone how it's supposed to go.
reversed: You have committed to a project without honestly assessing your current level, or you are attempting moves in conditions — skin, weather, fatigue — that are not in your favour. The step is real but the timing is not. Come back when you are ready, not when you are impatient.

upright: Everything required for the send is on the table — the fitness, the skin, the conditions, the memorised sequence. The Magician's wand points upward and his other hand points down: what you have trained is ready to be expressed on the rock. This is not the session to conserve energy or second-guess the beta. Every hold is accounted for. Trust what you have built.
reversed: The tools are present but something is misaligned — you are attempting the problem with tired forearms, or the sequence you rehearsed does not match what the rock is actually offering. The four suits lie scattered. Something needs to be consolidated before the attempt counts.

upright: The rock knows something you do not yet. The High Priestess sits between the pillars with the scroll in her lap — not everything in a problem can be decoded through observation or borrowed beta. Some sequences reveal themselves only through touch, through weight, through the quiet moment when you stop thinking and let your body read what your eyes have missed. Stop watching. Start feeling.
reversed: You are ignoring what your body has been telling you. The tweak that appeared two sessions ago, the shoulder that loads differently on underclings, the foot that slips every time on that smear — information is being withheld from your awareness because acknowledging it would mean stopping. The veil is up. It is not protecting you.

upright: Movement is coming easily. Problems that once felt foreign are beginning to feel like language — your body finds the line before your mind has named it. The Empress is surrounded by abundance that grew because it was tended consistently, not forced. Something you trained through winter is flowering now. Let the session be long. Let it be generous. This is what the work was for.
reversed: You are trying to climb through a creative or physical block by sheer repetition. The same sequence, the same attempt, the same fall — the Empress reversed asks whether the boulder problem you are staring at is the right one for this moment, or whether a different problem might unlock something that brute force cannot.

upright: Structure is serving you. A training plan, a consistent schedule, a systematic approach to projecting — these are not constraints on climbing, they are the architecture that allows you to climb harder for longer. The Emperor's throne is built on stone. Know your rest days. Know your limit days. Build the structure before you need it.
reversed: Rigidity has replaced discipline. You are following a training protocol that does not fit the season your body is in, or you are refusing to adjust a sequence on a problem because it is the sequence you committed to, even as the rock is showing you a different way. The orb and sceptre require wisdom to wield, not just authority.

upright: There is something to learn from the climber who has been on this wall longer than you. Not their beta necessarily — bodies are different, proportions are different — but their knowledge of the rock, of the conditions, of what this particular type of movement demands. The Hierophant's two keys unlock doors that YouTube cannot open. Ask. Watch. Climb with people who are better than you and remain curious rather than defensive.
reversed: Convention has become an obstacle. You are climbing a problem the way it was first climbed — the established beta, the approved sequence — when your body type, your strengths, your specific reach might open a better line entirely. The monks kneel before a tradition that doesn't account for you. Find your own way up.

upright: A choice is before you: the project that would push you into genuinely new territory, or the circuit that feels comfortable and confirms what you already know. The Lovers card is not about what is easier — it is about what is more honest. The angel above both paths does not choose. The blessing comes regardless. But only one direction leads to growth you haven't yet imagined.
reversed: You are in a climbing relationship — a partnership, a regular session group, a gym community — where the dynamic has started to work against your development. You may be staying because the comfort of familiar partners outweighs the discomfort of climbing differently. Examine what you are getting from the arrangement, and what it is costing you.

upright: You have been working this problem with discipline — mapping the sequence, building the specific strength, arriving to sessions with skin in condition and a clear mind. The Chariot holds two forces in tension and drives them forward. The send is not accidental. It is the result of holding opposing pressures — power and precision, commitment and control — in balance long enough to move through the crux. The finish hold is real. Go.
reversed: The attempt is out of control — too much force on a move that requires finesse, or too much hesitation on a move that requires commitment. The sphinxes are pulling apart. Step off, rest, and identify the one move where the breakdown is actually happening before you attempt again.

upright: The crux is not a strength problem. The Strength card shows a woman opening a lion's mouth with calm hands, no weapon, no force — only the kind of quiet confidence that cannot be performed under pressure, only inhabited. The hold is there. The foot is there. The move works when you stop fighting it and start moving through it. Breathe before you leave the last good hold. The lion does not require overpowering.
reversed: You are either timid where commitment is needed, or you are muscling through moves that your technique should be solving. The lion is not tamed by exhaustion. Consider whether the intensity you are bringing to the problem is a strategy or a way of avoiding the more frightening act of trusting your feet.

upright: The Hermit climbs alone on his mountain, lantern raised — not to be seen, but to see clearly. A solo session, early in the morning or late when the gym is quiet, can return something that crowded sessions take away. No one to perform for. No one else's beta to cloud your reading of the rock. The light you carry is yours. Use this session to find out what you actually know.
reversed: You have been isolating from the climbing community in a way that is limiting your development, or conversely, you have not had a single session of uninterrupted focus in weeks because the social pull of the gym consumes the time. The lantern is dimming. Find the conditions in which you actually climb your best, and protect them.

upright: The conditions cycle. Skin heals and thins and heals again. Fitness peaks and requires recovery before the next peak. The Wheel of Fortune turns and the four creatures at the corners hold their books open — the laws of physical adaptation do not change regardless of how urgently you want to be stronger now. Position yourself for the turn. The high point of your current cycle is close. Be ready.
reversed: You are forcing a session in a part of the cycle where rest would serve you better, or you are resting when your body is ready to work hard and you have talked yourself out of it. The wheel has turned and you are holding the spoke. Adapt.

upright: The grade is what it is. Justice holds both the sword and the scales — there is no benefit in climbing a soft problem and calling it harder than it is, and no benefit in dismissing a genuine send because you decided the grade was sandbagged. Honest assessment of where you are is the only foundation on which real progress builds. What you have climbed will be seen. What you have claimed will also be seen.
reversed: The grading conversation has become dishonest — either through ego, or through the opposite tendency to undervalue what you have actually done. The scales are tipped. Grade inflation and grade sandbagging both obscure something important: the actual level of movement you are capable of. Return to climbing the problem and leave the number alone for now.

upright: Step away from the project. The Hanged Man chose the tree; he was not placed there. His expression is serene, the halo around his head illuminated — this suspension is not defeat, it is reorientation. Come back in a week. Come back with fresh eyes and a different body position and the move that made no sense will sometimes reveal itself in the first attempt after the rest. Some problems are solved by not trying them.
reversed: You have been resting the project for so long that the rest has become avoidance. The conditions are good. Your skin is good. The excuses have run out. Come down from the tree.

upright: A project you have invested months in is coming to a close — either through the send or through the honest recognition that this problem, at this point in your development, is not the right one. Death rides a white horse and carries a white rose. The ending is not a failure. The movement patterns you built on this wall, the specific strength that this style demanded, will serve you on the next problem. Let it end. What you become next is built on everything you learned here.
reversed: You are refusing to let go of a project that is no longer serving your development — returning to it out of stubbornness or sunk cost rather than genuine desire. The card reversed does not spare you the transition. It only delays it. Some projects are not meant to be sent by you, at this time, in this body. That is not a verdict on your ability. It is information.

upright: Temperance stands at the water's edge, one foot on land and one in the stream — perfectly balanced, neither grasping nor retreating. This is the card of the climber who trains hard without destroying their tendons, who sessions consistently without overcooking their skin, who pushes on the project without losing the joy that brought them to the wall in the first place. The two cups flow between each other without spilling. You have found the rhythm. Protect it.
reversed: The balance has gone. You are climbing through pain that should be respected, or you have been so cautious that the adaptation you need is not happening. The out-of-balance climber trains hard for six weeks and then is injured for four months. The pattern repeats. Find the sustainable pace before the body imposes its own rest.

upright: The grade is the chain. The Devil's figures wear their chains loosely — they could be removed. You are free to climb for the movement, for the problem-solving, for the community, for the feeling of being strong and precise in your body. But the pull of the number is real, and if you are honest, it has at some point made you choose a gym tick over a beautiful outdoor problem, or a familiar grade over a movement style that would teach you something. The chains are not locked. You already know this.
reversed: You are stepping free — from a grade obsession that was making climbing joyless, from a comparison habit that made every session a performance review, from a tick list that had replaced genuine curiosity about movement. Be careful that freedom from one attachment does not immediately become attachment to a different metric. Climb what interests you.

upright: The pop is unexpected. You were certain the hold would stick, certain the sequence was dialled, and then the foot cut or the crimp broke position and the fall happened before you could prepare for it. The Tower's crown falls from the summit. Something you thought was solid was not. A training approach, a project strategy, a belief about what your body can do — something requires complete revision before you return. What rises from this is more honest than what stood before.
reversed: You can see the breakdown coming and you have time to adjust. A niggle that is trending toward injury, a sequence that is fundamentally wrong but you haven't committed to changing, a training block that is accumulating fatigue faster than it is building strength. The lightning is still in the clouds. Make the change before the fall makes it for you.

upright: After the injury, after the long break, after the session that made you wonder why you bother — the Star appears. A problem catches your eye from across the gym or across the hillside and something in you responds before your mind has assessed the grade or the style. The figure kneels at the water's edge and pours without grasping. This is what it feels like when climbing calls you rather than compels you. Follow it. The eight-pointed star does not promise an easy send. It promises a direction worth moving in.
reversed: You have temporarily lost the thread — the reason you climb, the movement that excited you, the project that once felt like yours. This is not permanent. But reconnecting requires something simpler than more training: find one problem that makes you curious and pull on it without expectation. The star is there. You are standing in the wrong place to see it.

upright: The Moon illuminates the crag just enough to see the next hold and not enough to see whether the sequence works. The problem you are projecting has sections you do not fully understand — a foot placement that might be wrong, a body position that might open a better option, a hold that might be oriented differently than you think. The wolf and the dog howl at the same light from different angles. Do not assume your current reading of this wall is the final one. Something is still hidden.
reversed: The fog is lifting. A sequence that resisted understanding for sessions is beginning to clarify — either through a different body position, a change in conditions, or simply enough attempts that the rock has revealed what it was withholding. What you feared about the problem may have been projection. What was genuinely difficult can now be addressed directly.

upright: Everything is working. The conditions are sharp, the skin is good, the body feels light, and the movement on problems that were recently near your limit feels almost casual. The Sun shines without apology on a child who rides without fear. This is a peak fitness window — rare, temporary, and worth treating with intention. Choose your projects accordingly. The problems you attempt in this window can shape what becomes possible in the next cycle.
reversed: The peak has passed or hasn't arrived yet. The session that felt like it should be a send attempt felt flat — the skin is wrong, or the body is heavy, or something is just slightly off. The Sun is behind a cloud. Rest. The window will open again. Don't burn good skin on a bad day.

upright: A reckoning arrives — an honest look at where your climbing actually is, what your body is genuinely capable of, and whether what you have been telling yourself about your level matches the evidence of your sends and your falls. The angel's trumpet is not a judgement. It is an invitation to rise from the comfortable story and climb from what is actually true. The past attempts, even the failures, have been preparing you for a more honest and therefore more powerful relationship with your climbing.
reversed: You have received information — from a coach, a partner, your own body — that you have not yet acted on. A movement pattern that is inefficient, a fear that is limiting your range, a training approach that is not producing what it once did. The coffins remain closed. The invitation is still open. Acknowledge what you know.

upright: The project is done. Not just sent — understood. The World dancer moves inside the laurel wreath at the completion of a full cycle: the first touch, the confusion, the specific training, the near misses, the rest, the send. You have not just climbed a hard problem. You have developed something that will change what is possible on the next one. The four creatures at the corners have witnessed the whole arc. Stand at the finish hold for a moment before you look for the next project. This one is complete.
reversed: You are nearly there and something is preventing the final step — a single move that won't consolidate, a fear that appears exactly when the send is possible, a fitness gap that needs one more training block. The wreath is within reach. Identify the one thing that remains and address only that. The rest is already done.

upright: The sequence clicks. Not gradually — suddenly, completely, the way a cipher resolves when the right key is applied. The Ace of Swords cuts through the fog of a problem you have been misreading: the foot that belongs two centimetres higher, the hip that wants to open rather than close, the hold that is an undercling not a sidepull. This insight arrived through contact with the rock, not through watching someone else climb it. Write it in your body before you rest.
reversed: You are overthinking the beta on a problem that rewards instinct over analysis. Or the clarity has arrived and it is uncomfortable — it reveals that the sequence you have committed to is wrong, that the approach you defended to your session partner will not work, and that starting over is now the honest path. The sword cuts in both directions.

upright: Two beta options and you cannot commit to either. The blindfolded figure holds both swords in balance at the water's edge — perfectly still and perfectly stuck. The left-hand start and the right-hand start both have advocates, both have logic, and the only way to know is to try one fully rather than oscillating between them across twenty half-attempts. Call it. Climb it. Adjust from evidence, not from further deliberation.
reversed: The stalemate has broken. A hold orientation you dismissed is worth trying, or a partner has shown you something that tips the decision. The blindfold is coming off. The water behind the figure represents what you were choosing not to see. Now that you can see it, commit to the direction it points.

upright: Something painful has entered the session — a hold has broken on a project you had dialled, a tweak has arrived in a finger that was already being managed carefully, a send attempt that should have gone ended in a fall that exposed how much further the problem is than you believed. The Three of Swords does not soften it: the heart is pierced, the rain is falling. Acknowledge the loss honestly. Suppressed climbing grief becomes a different kind of injury.
reversed: You are beginning to recover — from the injury that took you off the wall, from the project that broke your heart, from the long plateau that made you question whether you were improving at all. The swords are being withdrawn slowly. This is not the session where you return to full capacity. It is the session where returning becomes imaginable again.

upright: The Four of Swords is a tomb, not a grave — the knight rests beneath a stained-glass window, sword sheathed, three more hanging above him but not falling. Rest is not the absence of training. It is the phase in which adaptation actually occurs. The skin that is papering, the finger that is complaining, the forearms that have not fully recovered between sessions — these are not obstacles to progress. They are the body communicating the schedule it requires. The window above him is still lit. Rest inside it.
reversed: You cannot rest. The conditions are perfect, the project is calling, and two days off feels like two weeks of fitness lost. Or you have rested so long that the return feels frightening — the level you were at before the break seeming further away than it actually is. The knight must eventually rise. The problems will wait. You will not climb well if you don't lie down.

upright: The tick came with a cost. A take on a move you hadn't consolidated, a knee-bar that drained the crux of its meaning, a beta that bypassed the intended sequence in a way that left you knowing the problem is not truly done. The Five of Swords shows a figure collecting swords while others walk away — the victory is real and the room is emptier for it. The problem is your problem. The standard you set on it is also yours. Consider what you actually collected today.
reversed: A session that ended in conflict — a disputed grade, a disagreement about beta ethics, a moment where competition for a problem became something less than climbing — is finding resolution. The Five reversed suggests that rebuilding what was damaged is possible if someone goes first. The swords are not worth what the tension is costing.

upright: You are moving — to a new gym, a new crag, a new style that the problems where you have been spending your time cannot teach you. The Six of Swords shows a ferryman, a cloaked figure, a child, and six upright swords embedded in the hull of the boat. You carry the learned patterns with you; they will land at the new wall before you do. The water ahead is not without difficulty. It is calmer than what you are leaving, and it goes somewhere.
reversed: You want to leave but haven't, or you have moved but brought the same habits with you. A new gym does not automatically produce a new climber. The movement patterns that limit you at one wall will limit you at the next unless they are addressed directly. Unfinished business travels in the hull alongside the swords.

upright: The Seven of Swords figure carries most of the swords away quietly, looking back over his shoulder. In climbing this card asks about honesty — the send that included a dab, the redpoint that had a rest on the rope, the tick that went into the logbook while something in you knew it wasn't clean. These are small deceptions and they compound quietly. The problem you are actually working on is the relationship between your standards and your actions. The rock does not care. You do.
reversed: You are choosing to redo a problem rather than log the impure send. Or an admission that something wasn't clean — to a partner, in a logbook, to yourself — has cleared something that was quietly accumulating. The integrity of your climbing is yours to define. The Seven reversed is the moment you return to the wall and do it right.

upright: You are not stuck because the problem is impossible. You are stuck because the story about the problem has become more fixed than the problem itself. The Eight of Swords figure stands bound and blindfolded in shallow water, surrounded by swords that have been placed — not thrown, not closing in. The constraint is real and it is also, in part, constructed. Remove the story that you cannot do this style of climbing. Try the move without the verdict already rendered.
reversed: The self-imposed ceiling is lifting. A move you had categorised as beyond you has been done — tentatively, sloppily, but done — and the category is no longer accurate. The Eight reversed is not a dramatic breakthrough. It is the quiet revision of a belief that was never as permanent as it felt. Step forward from the revised position.

upright: The Nine of Swords is three in the morning before a competition, before an outdoor project session with an audience, before the attempt on a problem that matters too much. The figure sits up in the dark, nine swords horizontal on the wall above them. The fall you are imagining is larger than the actual fall. The failure you are rehearsing has more consequence in the mind than it will have on the mat. Name the specific fear. Vague dread is always larger than what is inside it.
reversed: The anxiety is releasing. The competition is over, the attempt happened, the fear was larger than the event — or you have found a way to work with the fear of falling rather than around it. The Nine reversed does not mean the problem is solved. It means the acute grip has loosened enough to climb through it.

upright: The injury is real. Ten swords in the back is not a metaphor for a slight niggle — this is a pulley, a shoulder, something that requires you to stop fully and attend to it properly. The Ten of Swords figure lies at the water's edge beneath a brightening sky. The sea is calm. This ending is absolute, which means it is also clear. What the recovery period teaches you about training, about patience, about the parts of your climbing that do not require your fingers will change what you return to.
reversed: You are returning — carefully, incrementally, with more respect for the body's timeline than you had before the injury. Or you are refusing to accept an ending that needs to happen: climbing through pain that should be rested, turning a minor injury into a major one through refusal to stop. The swords remain in the figure who will not acknowledge the ground. Let the recovery be complete before the return.

upright: The Page of Swords stands on high ground in the wind, sword raised, eyes alert — watching everything before committing to anything. This is the climber who is new enough to a style or a crag to be genuinely curious: watching how more experienced climbers weight their feet, where they look before they move, what they do with their hips on a move that looks impossible from the ground. This observational phase is not wasted time. It is reading a text before attempting to write in it.
reversed: The watching has replaced the climbing. Too much beta-watching, too much video analysis, too much time spent on what a move should look like and not enough spent learning through contact with the rock. The Page reversed also appears when you are speaking with more confidence about climbing than your experience yet justifies. Climb the problem. Form the opinion after.

upright: The Knight of Swords charges at full gallop, visor down, committed entirely to the direction of travel. Some moves require exactly this — the dyno that punishes hesitation, the deadpoint that requires you to be already moving when you leave the hold, the sloper that only works when you commit to the position rather than approach it cautiously. The energy is correct. Check once that the mat is where it needs to be. Then go without reservation.
reversed: A move executed with too much speed and not enough precision has resulted in a miss, a swing, a fall that could have been avoided. Or the Knight has been charging at the crux move repeatedly without pausing to diagnose what is actually going wrong. Speed is not the same as effectiveness. Slow the sequence down until you understand it, then rebuild the speed from understanding.

upright: The Queen of Swords has seen difficulty and it has made her precise rather than bitter. She reads the problem as it is — not the problem she wishes it were, not the problem that would suit her style. Her blade is upright and her hand is open: honest in assessment, clear in execution, direct in the feedback she gives and receives. This is the climber who knows exactly where they are in their development and uses that knowledge as a tool rather than a verdict.
reversed: The precision has curdled. Feedback from a partner or a coach is landing as criticism rather than information, or your assessment of the problem has become so fixed that you cannot see what the rock is actually offering. The Queen reversed uses the sword to defend rather than to clarify. What disappointment are you carrying that is making honest engagement feel threatening?

upright: The King of Swords sits upright in a clear sky, sword vertical, authority derived from experience rather than assertion. This is the climber who has been on enough rock to know when a style demands strength and when it demands surrender, when a grade is honest and when it is not, when a body needs rest and when the hesitation is fear rather than wisdom. If someone with this quality of judgment is available to you at the crag or the gym, climb with them. Listen more than you speak.
reversed: Experience is being wielded as authority rather than offered as knowledge. The climber who has been doing this longer is telling you that your beta is wrong, that your grade assessment is inflated, that your approach is mistaken — possibly correctly, but in a way that closes the conversation rather than opening it. Expertise that cannot be questioned becomes orthodoxy. Orthodoxy does not teach.

upright: Something is igniting — a new area you have driven past for months and finally stopped at, a style you have been avoiding because it exposes weakness, a project that caught your eye from the ground and hasn't let go since. The Ace of Wands is a living branch still sprouting leaves, held from cloud. The fire is real and it is new. Pull on the problem before you ask anyone what the grade is. Before the session becomes a project, let it be a discovery.
reversed: The spark didn't catch, or it caught and burned through before anything was built. A new project that generated excitement for two sessions has been quietly abandoned. This reversal asks whether the flame was weak or whether the conditions were wrong — too much skin, too little time, too many other commitments crowding the space where fire needs air. Some seasons require clearing before something new can start.

upright: You have climbed everything this wall or this area has to offer at your current level, and you are standing at the edge looking out at what comes next. The Two of Wands figure holds a globe in one hand and a staff in the other, surveying the horizon from the ramparts of what he has already built. A new crag, a harder grade range, a different discipline — the world in your hand is small but the implication is significant. The planning season has arrived. Begin it seriously.
reversed: The vision is real and the plan is not. You know roughly where you want to go — a specific crag, a grade milestone, a trip — and have not committed to the preparation it requires. Or fear has you watching others set out for the objectives you have circled in the guidebook while you convince yourself the timing is not right. The globe does not get lighter from holding it at the wall.

upright: You have put in the training and now you are standing at the cliff watching the results arrive. The Three of Wands figure stands with their back to us, patient and confident, watching the horizon. A training cycle that felt abstract in the gym is now expressing itself on real rock — moves that were at your absolute limit are becoming moves you can do. Let the season develop. Your ships are on the horizon. They are coming.
reversed: Something you prepared for has not materialised on schedule. A trip fell through, a fitness peak didn't arrive when expected, or a project you travelled to is not going to go in the time you have. The Three reversed asks whether the preparation was adequate or whether the timeline was yours to control in the first place. Some objectives require more seasons than one.

upright: The project is done. Not just sent — properly done, on good terms, in good conditions, with people who understand what it meant. The Four of Wands is a celebration beneath a canopy of flowers, four staffs planted firmly in the earth. Something has closed completely and the closing is worth marking together. The climbing community you have been part of through this project — the partners who spotted, the people who watched, the climbers who shared the wall with you — let them be part of this moment. You built the staffs together.
reversed: The celebration is premature or the stability underneath it is not what it appears. A send that felt complete has a question attached — conditions that were marginal, a move that wasn't fully in control, the quiet knowledge that you would not repeat it today in the same way. Or the stability of your climbing foundation is less solid than recent results suggest. The garlands are up. Check what the staffs are standing in.

upright: The crowded boulder problem, the competition format, the session where three climbers are all working the same line and the dynamic has become something other than climbing — the Five of Wands shows figures in apparent conflict, wands raised, but no one is injured and the energy, managed well, is generative. Competition sharpens. Watching others' beta teaches. Sharing a project with climbers of different styles produces solutions none of you would have found alone. The conflict is the friction. Use it.
reversed: The competition has become corrosive. A dynamic at the wall — a person who monopolises a problem, a group that makes others feel unwelcome, an unspoken contest for status dressed as casual climbing — has made a session feel like something other than climbing. The Five reversed asks what is not being named. Unacknowledged competition does not dissolve. It shapes the culture of the space.

upright: The send happened in front of people and they witnessed it. The Victor rides through the crowd, the laurel wreath on the wand. Accept this with ease — not deflecting, not performing false modesty, not immediately minimising the grade. People who climb understand what they watched. Receive what is being offered. Those who were there for the attempts are also there for this. Let them have it alongside you.
reversed: A send that deserved acknowledgment went unwitnessed, or the recognition you received felt hollow because it came from people who didn't understand what the problem actually demanded. The Six reversed can also arrive as a warning: how much of your motivation to climb this specific problem was the audience rather than the climbing? Examine what you were actually pursuing before you look for the next project.

upright: You are in the crux and you are pumped and the instinct is to rush. The Seven of Wands shows a figure on high ground, one staff raised, six coming up from below — the position is defensible but the effort is real. You have earned the high ground on this route. You have the sequence. Stay in your body. Breathe on the rest before the crux sequence. The endurance is there. The problem is whether you trust it enough to use it slowly rather than frantically.
reversed: You are losing the hold — not because the move is impossible, but because the fatigue has crossed the threshold where good movement is available. The Seven reversed sometimes signals the wisdom of stepping off rather than grinding through a pumped attempt that embeds bad movement patterns. Come down. Shake out. Go again when the arms have something to offer.

upright: Eight wands crossing the sky in parallel — this is the session where everything moves. The project that has been static for three sessions suddenly has a crux that makes sense. Problems that were at your limit feel accessible. The body is recovered, the skin is good, the conditions are sharp, and movement is happening faster than analysis can track it. The Eight of Wands carries no figure — it is pure momentum. Attempt the project today. When the velocity arrives, it does not wait for you to decide you are ready.
reversed: The momentum has stalled. Conditions that were forecast to be good are not. The skin is thinner than expected. The session that was supposed to produce the send is producing frustration instead. The wands have stopped mid-flight. Identify whether the obstacle is external — conditions, fatigue, skin — or whether something in your preparation is the actual bottleneck. Either way, one thing is blocking everything else. Address only that.

upright: The Nine of Wands shows a figure who has clearly been through something — bandaged head, leaning on a staff, eight more wands upright behind him like a fence he constructed from previous attempts. He is not defeated. He is guarded, experienced, and still standing. You have taken falls on this problem that hurt your confidence more than your body. You have been close enough to feel the finish hold without touching it. You are still here. The wariness is earned. One more attempt, from what you actually know now, is different from all the previous ones.
reversed: The accumulated attempts have become a weight rather than a resource. You are approaching the problem with the memory of every failure rather than the knowledge every attempt produced. Or the commitment required for one more serious try is genuinely beyond what is available today — not as defeat but as honest accounting. The project will still be there. Come back when the figure can stand upright without leaning on the staff.

upright: The Ten of Wands figure leans forward under the weight of ten staffs, head down, the destination visible but the load enormous. The project that was exciting three months ago has become something you feel obligated to rather than drawn to. The training sessions scheduled around it, the trips planned for it, the conversations about it — somewhere the climbing became secondary to the project as an identity. Put some of the staffs down. Return to climbing problems that ask nothing of you except movement. The project will still be there when the load is lighter.
reversed: Something is being set down — the project that became a burden, the grade goal that was making every session a performance, the expectation that climbing should always be progression rather than sometimes just climbing. The staffs hit the floor. Notice how many there were. Before you pick any of them back up, decide which ones actually belong to you.

upright: The Page of Wands stands in an open landscape with a staff taller than himself, studying the salamander embroidered on his tunic — alert, curious, not yet certain of direction. Everything is interesting. The overhang and the slab, the gym and the crag, the crimp and the sloper. This early-season curiosity, this willingness to be a beginner in styles where you have no competence yet, is a resource. Do not rush to specialise. The problems that make you feel least capable are showing you exactly where the growth is.
reversed: Enthusiasm is scattered across every new thing and nothing is being developed. A different area every weekend, a new project started before the last one was understood, technique videos watched without the hours of movement practice that would make them mean something. The Page reversed is not without fire — the fire is real. It needs a single direction to build into something.

upright: The Knight of Wands travels for climbing. He has driven through the night to be at a crag in good conditions, packed a van for a month in a place where the rock is everything he needs, committed to a trip before the logistics were entirely worked out because the window was open and waiting is its own kind of loss. The horse is barely touching the ground. The energy is correct. The move requires this kind of wholehearted approach. Check the forecast. Go.
reversed: The charge has been impulsive and the consequences are arriving. A trip booked in peak skin-destroying humidity, a project committed to before the prerequisite strength was built, a training block begun with intensity that is not sustainable past week two. The Knight reversed asks for less momentum and more preparation. The destination is right. The pace needs adjusting.

upright: The Queen of Wands sits squarely on her throne with a sunflower in one hand, a black cat at her feet, and a quality of presence that does not require anyone to acknowledge it. This is the climber who moves through the gym without performing — who helps someone with beta without making them feel small, who is visibly strong without using that strength to establish hierarchy, who brings warmth to a space that can easily become competitive. The sunflower faces the light. So does everything in her orbit.
reversed: The confidence is performance rather than foundation. A sharp comment about someone else's grade, a deliberate display of ability in front of a climber who is struggling, the need to be seen as the strongest person at the crag — the Queen of Wands reversed is insecurity wearing the costume of ease. The black cat has turned its back. Something underneath the display needs attending to.

upright: The King of Wands sits forward on his throne, not resting into it — ready, present, the cloak of salamanders around him marking someone who has lived inside the fire long enough to understand it. He has climbed enough seasons to know that the hardest problems are not always the most important ones, that the climber who inspires a room is not always the strongest, that what you build in a community outlasts what you send on any wall. If you are in a position to shape how others experience climbing, do it with the generosity this card asks for.
reversed: Passion has become possession. The King reversed claims ownership of a problem, a style, a local crag — treating the climbing community as something to dominate rather than serve. Or the vision has become reckless: bold objectives pursued without the preparation they require, inspiring language that doesn't translate into honest mentorship. The salamanders on the cloak are restless. The fire needs directing, not just embodying.

upright: Something is opening that has nothing to do with grade. A problem catches you in a way that is entirely about movement — the way the sequence flows from one hold to the next, the way a particular body position feels unexpectedly elegant, the satisfaction of a move that required no force at all. The Ace of Cups is a chalice overflowing, held from cloud, a dove descending. What is being offered here is not a tick. It is a reminder of why you came to the wall in the first place. Receive it.
reversed: The cup is upturned. Climbing has felt mechanical for longer than is sustainable — problem after problem without the quality of attention that makes it worth doing. The well has run dry. This is not a fitness problem or a grade problem. It is a question of why, and the answer requires honesty rather than more training volume.

upright: A climbing partnership is forming that is more than logistical. Two figures exchange cups beneath the caduceus — what flows between them is not just shared transport and belaying. A partner who makes you try harder by being present, who reads your movement honestly and tells you what they see, who knows when to offer beta and when to stay quiet while you figure it out. This relationship will take you to problems you would not have found or attempted alone. Tend it.
reversed: The climbing partnership has become unequal or is quietly working against your development. One person is always projecting while the other waits, or the dynamic has drifted into one person leading and the other following without it ever being discussed. The cups are no longer meeting at the same level. Name what has shifted before the imbalance becomes the shape of the partnership.

upright: The send happened and people were there. Three figures raise their cups — no one is leading the celebration, the joy is distributed equally. The community that surrounds your climbing, that shares the mat with you, that has watched the attempts and absorbed the falls — let them be part of this. The bonds formed at the base of a hard problem carry through seasons. The celebration is not separate from the climbing. It is part of what climbing is.
reversed: The community around a problem or a wall has become political. Someone is dominating the space in a way that makes it less welcoming. A send that should have been shared has become competitive. The celebration is happening but not everyone is invited — and the person who notices the absence most clearly is you. Something in the culture of this place needs addressing before it becomes the culture.

upright: You are sitting at the base of the problem, arms crossed, not really seeing it. The holds are there. The session is available. But something has saturated — too many attempts, too much thinking, too much time spent on a problem that no longer speaks to you the way it once did. The Four of Cups shows a hand emerging from a cloud offering a fourth cup to a figure who is looking away. An adjacent problem, a different wall, a completely new style is extending an invitation. Look up from the one you have been staring at.
reversed: Something has shifted and the wall is interesting again. The problem you had gone stale on has a fresh edge, or a different problem nearby has pulled your attention in a direction that has reawakened the session. The Four reversed is not a dramatic revelation. It is the simple act of looking up and finding something worth reaching for.

upright: Three cups are spilled. A trip that was planned around a specific objective and the objective did not go. A hold that broke. A season cut short. The Five of Cups figure stands over what is lost in a dark cloak, unable yet to turn and see the two cups still standing behind them. The grief is legitimate — do not rush it. But at some point, look behind you. The movement you developed on the approach, the strength built in preparation, the partners who were there — two cups are still standing. They hold something real.
reversed: You are beginning to turn. The failed trip is becoming a story you can tell without bitterness. The injury that took you off the wall is becoming a chapter rather than a verdict. The two remaining cups are coming into focus. The bridge in the background of the Five of Cups leads somewhere. You can see it from where you are standing now.

upright: A crag you climbed at years ago, a style you learned on before you had opinions about it, a movement pattern from early in your climbing that your body still knows. The Six of Cups is the card of what was genuinely good and is now being offered again — not as nostalgia, but as resource. Sometimes the most productive thing a climber can do is return to the basics they outgrew too quickly. Some movement knowledge does not expire. Some old problems still have things to teach.
reversed: You are living in a previous version of your climbing. A grade range you used to inhabit that now feels safe, a crag that asks nothing new of you, a style you can perform without being present. The Six of Cups reversed arrives when the past is being used as a refuge rather than a reference. What was genuinely good then does not require reinstating now.

upright: Seven cups hang in the clouds, each containing something different — a castle, a wreath, a dragon, a jewel, a shrouded figure, a ghost, a snake. This is the climber paralysed by possibility: every crag in the guidebook, every grade range, every style all equally compelling and therefore none of them pursued. Exploration has value. At some point exploration becomes avoidance of the discomfort of committing to one thing and finding out what you are actually made of. Pick one cup. Find out what is actually inside it.
reversed: The fog is clearing. A direction is emerging — a specific crag, a specific style, a specific grade range that feels genuinely right rather than arbitrarily chosen. The Seven reversed is the moment you pick up one cup and pull on the problem rather than continuing to circle it. The choice will not be perfect. It will be real, which is better.

upright: You are leaving a wall, a gym, a crag, a climbing community that has given you real things and no longer gives you what you need. The Eight of Cups figure departs at night, under a moon that illuminates just enough to walk by. Eight cups are stacked neatly behind them — not thrown, not broken, complete. The next crag is darker than this one and further away and worth going toward. You are not running from something. You are walking toward the thing that the current place cannot offer.
reversed: You are staying when leaving would serve your climbing, or you have moved on physically but carried the same patterns with you. A new gym does not automatically produce a new climber. A new crag does not reset the movement habits that are limiting you. What you need to leave behind is not always a place.

upright: The Nine of Cups is the wish card — the figure sits with arms crossed and nine cups arranged behind them like a trophy shelf. The send you trained for has happened. The grade you set your season around is in the logbook. This card gives you permission to feel this fully before reaching for the next thing. The cups are yours. You put them there. The next project can wait one session while you sit with what this one meant.
reversed: The external marker is present and the internal satisfaction is not. The grade was reached and within a week it felt like the new baseline. The send was logged and the feeling was smaller than the effort that preceded it. The Nine of Cups reversed asks what you are actually seeking beneath the goals you set — and whether the number could ever have delivered it. Climb something that has no grade attached for a while. See what that teaches you.

upright: A rare and complete season — the fitness arrived, the conditions cooperated, the partnerships were good, the objectives were met, and the climbing felt like climbing rather than like work. The Ten of Cups is the rainbow arching over the landscape, everything accounted for. Recognise this as the exception rather than the standard and protect it accordingly. Do not introduce unnecessary complexity into something that is working. The harmony is real. Let it be what it is.
reversed: The picture of harmony has something unresolved beneath it. A season that looked successful from outside had a cost that was paid quietly — a relationship in the climbing community that frayed, a body that was pushed past what was honest, a joy that was performed more than felt. Look at what held the rainbow up. Make sure it is sustainable.

upright: The Page of Cups holds a chalice and a fish has appeared inside it — impossible, unexpected, entirely real. Stay open. The session that was supposed to be routine has produced something surprising: a movement solution you found by accident that reframes a category of problem you thought you understood, a hold used in a way no one showed you, a sequence that arrived through play rather than analysis. The fish is real. This discovery is worth more than the tick it came attached to.
reversed: The sensitivity has become fragility. Feedback about your movement is landing as judgement about your potential. A session partner's observation — offered with care — has closed you rather than opened you. Or the playfulness that makes bouldering generative has been replaced by seriousness that makes every attempt a test. The Page reversed still has the cup. The fish has retreated. Recover the lightness.

upright: The Knight of Cups rides slowly, deliberately, visor up, a cup held before him as an offering. This is not the reckless charge of a climber trying to prove something. This is the climber who chooses a project because the movement genuinely calls to them, who spends a session on a problem that will never be their hardest send because the style teaches them something they cannot get anywhere else. The horse moves on water. The path is not guaranteed. The direction is honest. Go anyway.
reversed: The romantic vision of a project has not survived contact with the actual climbing. The problem looked beautiful from the ground and is awkward and unpleasant on the wall. Or the emotional investment in a specific objective is so high that the falls on it feel disproportionately devastating. The Knight reversed asks whether you are climbing the problem or whether you are in a relationship with an idea about the problem.

upright: The Queen of Cups sits at the water's edge with an ornate closed cup that only she can see into. Her intuition about climbing — about what a body needs, about when a session is done, about which problem is right for this particular moment — is her primary instrument, and she has learned to trust it over the advice of training plans and outside opinion. If your body is telling you something about a tendon, a shoulder, a fatigue that doesn't resolve between sessions, this is the card that gives you permission to listen before the body escalates.
reversed: The intuition is being absorbed rather than applied. Every ache is being felt and processed privately and nothing is being changed. Or the boundary between your own experience and the experience of every climber around you has dissolved — you absorb the frustration of the person falling on the problem next to you, the anxiety of the person who hasn't sent in weeks, until you can no longer read your own body's signals. Find the distance from which care for others is possible without becoming unable to hear yourself.

upright: The King of Cups sits on his throne in open water — stable within the emotional currents of a climbing community that can be intense, competitive, injured, elated, and grieving all in the same session. He holds the cup and the sceptre simultaneously: feeling and authority together. This is the climbing mentor who knows when to push and when to hold back, who can sit with someone in a long plateau without fixing it prematurely, who has been through enough of their own difficult seasons to be genuinely useful in someone else's. The fish pendant says: he came from the deep. He knows what lives there.
reversed: The steadiness is being performed. The mentor who appears composed is carrying their own unacknowledged injuries — physical, emotional — and the performance of stability is preventing the people around them from offering what would actually help. Or the emotional intelligence is being used to manage others' perceptions of the climbing community rather than to honestly serve it. The water is moving. Acknowledge it.

upright: A real opportunity is being extended — a trip invitation, a coaching offer, access to a crag you have wanted to climb at, a training partnership with someone whose level would pull yours up. The Ace of Pentacles is a hand from cloud holding a single coin above a garden gate. This is not an idea. This is a concrete opening with a window. What grows through that gate will be proportional to what you commit once you step through it. Read the terms. Then go.
reversed: An opportunity arrived and the timing was wrong, or the preparation wasn't there, or the decision took too long and the window closed. The coin is still in the cloud — the potential has not vanished entirely — but the gate requires active movement toward it. Hesitation here has a cost that compounds.

upright: You are managing more than one significant climbing commitment simultaneously — a project and a training block, an outdoor season and a competition cycle, performance climbing and injury rehabilitation. The Two of Pentacles figure juggles two coins inside the lemniscate while ships rise and fall behind him. The balance is real and effortful. Something will eventually need to be prioritised. Trying to peak for everything at once produces peaks for nothing.
reversed: Something has been dropped. Skin that needed rest was climbed on and is now raw. A finger that needed a week off was trained through and has become a month off. The ships in the background are in rougher water. The cost of the dropped commitment is now more visible than the benefit of having kept everything moving. Stop, assess, and sequence what remains.

upright: Three craftsmen in the cathedral — architect, monk, sculptor — each contributing something the others cannot. A training partnership, a trip crew, a regular session group where the different strengths of different climbers produce movement solutions none of them would have reached alone. The climber who reads feet, the climber who reads hips, the climber who has been on this specific wall for ten years — all three are in the same session today. Show up. The cathedral is worth building and it requires all three.
reversed: The collaboration has fractured. Someone is giving unsolicited beta on every attempt, or the group dynamic has collapsed into parallel solo sessions that happen to share a mat. What should have been collaborative has become territorial. Revisit the dynamic — not to assign blame, but to recover the thing that made climbing together worth doing in the first place.

upright: You are holding what you have built — a grade range you can climb consistently, a training approach that is producing results, a set of movement patterns that feel reliable. The Four of Pentacles figure sits with a coin on his head, one under each foot, one against his chest. The city is behind him. Some seasons in climbing are consolidation seasons: not the time to reach for a new grade, but to deepen what the current one demands. Know which season this is and do not apologise for it.
reversed: The grip has loosened — on a grade range you were defending past its usefulness, on a training approach that stopped producing results two cycles ago, on a style that once defined your climbing but now only protects you from attempting something harder. The coin in the chest is being released. Something new becomes possible. Examine whether the release is chosen or imposed, and proceed accordingly.

upright: A difficult period — injury, a long plateau, loss of access to the crag that was the centre of your climbing life, the kind of financial pressure that makes trips and gym memberships feel impossible. The Five of Pentacles shows two figures moving through snow past a lit window. Neither looks up at the light. The window represents what is available — a training substitute, a community that would help if asked, a different form of climbing that the difficulty has made invisible. Look up from the hardship long enough to see what is still accessible.
reversed: The hardship is easing. The injury has a timeline now rather than an open end. The plateau has produced its first visible crack. Help that was available all along is finally being accepted. Receiving support from your climbing community is not a concession. It is how the figures finally get out of the snow.

upright: The Six of Pentacles shows a merchant with scales distributing coins to two kneeling figures. In climbing this card is about the exchange of knowledge — beta given freely, a crag introduced to someone new, time spent helping a less experienced climber work a problem rather than always working your own. The knowledge you share generously tends to return in forms you cannot predict. The scales are balanced when you remember that someone once stood where you are standing now and chose to give rather than withhold.
reversed: Knowledge is being used as currency rather than offered as gift. The climber who gives beta conditionally, who shares the good holds only with their inner circle, who treats local knowledge as power over newcomers rather than welcome into the community — the scales in the Six reversed are tipped and the figure holding them is aware of it. Examine what the withholding is protecting.

upright: You are mid-season, leaning on the fence, watching what the training has produced so far. The pentacles on the vine are visible but the harvest is not yet in. This is the session where honest assessment matters more than another attempt — are the specific strength gains you planned for arriving? Is the project responding to the approach you committed to? The farmer's rest is not laziness. It is the intelligence that adjusts the season before the season ends.
reversed: You expected more visible progress by now. The training was consistent, the sessions were real, and the project is not responding in the way you anticipated. Before you abandon the approach, consider: are you measuring too early, or did you prepare for the wrong demands? Some harvests require a different season, not more effort in this one.

upright: The craftsman sits alone at the bench, one pentacle after another produced with increasing precision. He is not distracted. This is the climber who drills the footwork on easy problems until it becomes automatic, who does the hangboard session even on the days when the fingers feel strong and pulling on hard things would feel better, who returns to the movement fundamentals that will underpin every hard send for the next five years. The coins on the wall behind him are evidence. Mastery accumulates in the repetitions that feel unnecessary.
reversed: The focus has fractured across too many training goals simultaneously — finger strength, endurance, technique, flexibility all being addressed in the same block with insufficient depth in any of them. Or the perfectionism has made the standard of good movement so high that nothing in a session counts. The craftsman reversed either cannot sit at the bench or cannot leave it. Both produce the same empty wall.

upright: The Nine of Pentacles shows a woman alone in a garden of her own making, a hooded falcon on her gloved hand, pentacles fruiting on the vines around her. She built this. She is enjoying it without requiring an audience. This card arrives when your climbing has reached a level of self-sufficiency — you can read a new crag, find your own beta, assess your own readiness, train without external direction. The falcon is disciplined skill held lightly. The garden is the body you have cultivated. Stand in it for a moment.
reversed: The self-sufficiency has become isolation, or the garden requires more maintenance than enjoyment. You are training alone when a community would accelerate your development, assessing your own climbing without the honest mirror that a good partner provides, or working so hard to maintain your level that the pleasure of being in a strong body has been entirely consumed by the effort of keeping it there. The falcon has not been unhooded in months.

upright: Legacy in climbing is not a scoreboard. The Ten of Pentacles shows three generations in an archway, ten pentacles arranged in the pattern of the Tree of Life — abundance that spans time, structure that outlasts the individual. What you build in a climbing community, the culture you help shape at a local crag, the climbers you introduce to movement that changes their relationship with their own bodies — this outlasts any grade you send. Build accordingly. The elder in the archway is not watching the scoreboard.
reversed: Something built to last has not. A crag that was well-managed has been damaged by overuse or poor ethics. A climbing community whose culture was carefully developed has eroded since the people who shaped it moved on or moved away. The Ten of Pentacles reversed asks what was built for longevity and what was built for visibility — and what the difference has cost.

upright: The Page of Pentacles holds a single coin at eye level in an open field, studying it with full attention before deciding what to do with it. A new training approach, a new movement concept, a crag you have never climbed at — the Page is not impatient. He is learning what he is holding before committing to a direction. This is the right posture at the start of something. Touch the holds before you plan the sequence. Understand the style before you judge whether you are good at it.
reversed: The studying has replaced the climbing. A new training methodology has been researched thoroughly and applied for three sessions before being replaced by the next one. The Page of Pentacles reversed accumulates knowledge about climbing faster than they accumulate time on the wall. The coin is being looked at, not used. Pick the smallest possible next action on the rock and take it today.

upright: The Knight of Pentacles sits on a still horse in a ploughed field, one coin held before him. Every other knight is moving. This one is not. He will move when he is ready, and when he does the furrow will be straight and will not need redoing. This is the climber who does not attempt a problem until the individual moves are understood, who does not add training volume until the current volume is fully absorbed, who does not travel to a hard objective until the prerequisite climbing is genuinely in place. The work is slower. The work holds.
reversed: Diligence has become rigidity. An approach that produced results in one phase of development is now the obstacle in the next — the same warm-up on the same problems, the same training structure applied to a body that has outgrown it, the same sequence on a project defended against new information the rock is offering. The horse is capable. The furrow needs to change.

upright: The Queen of Pentacles sits in her garden with a rabbit at her feet and a single coin held in her lap without display — material competence worn as ease rather than performance. This is the climber who manages their body with the same intelligence they bring to the rock: who knows when skin needs two days not one, who understands the difference between productive fatigue and accumulated damage, who plans a season with the same care they bring to projecting a problem. If this quality of self-stewardship is available to you, extend it without apology.
reversed: The care has been directed entirely outward. Skin is being monitored for everyone at the session except yourself. Rest is being recommended to every partner while your own rest days keep getting cancelled. The Queen of Pentacles reversed is not a failure of knowledge — she knows exactly what is needed. It is a failure to apply that knowledge inward. The garden needs tending. So does the gardener.

upright: The King of Pentacles sits on a throne carved with bulls, vines climbing the stone around him, abundance that was not inherited but accumulated through seasons of disciplined, patient work. This is not the flashiest climber in the gym. It is the one whose level has compounded steadily for ten years because every training decision was made for the long term, every injury was respected, every plateau was used to consolidate rather than escaped through recklessness. The vines grew slowly. They are now structural. This is what it looks like to have built something that lasts.
reversed: The accumulation has become the goal rather than the means. The King of Pentacles reversed is the climber who tracks every metric, logs every session, measures every finger force — and has lost the thread that connects all that data to the reason they climb. The vines have been stripped of their leaves for analysis. The throne is becoming a spreadsheet. Climb something today without recording it. See what returns.
